literal: Prince of Rencheng
idiomatic: The Prince of Rencheng

literal: Yun, Prince of Rencheng, was five years old when Gongzong died; he wept without cease.
idiomatic: Yun, Prince of Rencheng, was only five when Gongzong died, yet he wept without stopping.

literal: Shizu heard of it and summoned him, took him in his arms, and wept, saying: "How can you know enough to have the mind of a grown man!"
idiomatic: Shizu heard and called for him, took him in his arms, and wept. "How is it you already have a grown man's heart?"

literal: In the fifth year of Heping he was enfeoffed and appointed Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Grand General Who Conquers the East, and Grand General of Helong Garrison.
idiomatic: In Heping year 5 he received his fief and was made Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Grand General Who Conquers the East, and commander of Helong Garrison.

literal: Under Xianzu he was made commander of all military affairs within and without the court and Director of the Inner Palace at the Center, heard civil suits, and won great praise of the age.
idiomatic: Under Xianzu he commanded all armies at court and in the field, directed the Inner Palace at the Center, heard civil suits, and won wide renown.

literal: In Yanxing, Xianzu gathered the ministers and wished to abdicate to Zitui, Prince of Jingzhao.
idiomatic: In the Yanxing era Xianzu gathered his ministers, intending to abdicate to Zitui, Prince of Jingzhao.

literal: Kings, dukes, and grandees dared speak first of none.
idiomatic: Among kings, dukes, and grandees none dared speak first.

literal: Yun advanced and said: "Your Majesty is just now raising great peace and overseeing all within the seas—how could you go against the ancestral temples above and abandon the myriad people below?"
idiomatic: Yun stepped forward. "Your Majesty is raising an age of peace and holds all under heaven—how could you turn your back on the ancestral temples and cast off the people?"

literal: Father passing the throne to son has long been the way; since the rise of Imperial Wei there has been no change.
idiomatic: Father passing rule to son is an ancient way; since Imperial Wei rose, that line has never been broken.

literal: The heir apparent holds the orthodox succession; sagely virtue was long manifest.
idiomatic: The crown prince holds the orthodox succession; his sagely virtue was long plain to see.

literal: If Your Majesty truly wishes to set aside dusty affairs and nourish the spirit in clarity and distance, the charge of the heir should continue the precious succession; if you wish to discard the heir,[1] lightly to shift the imperial seat—I fear that is not the former sages' intent and will startle men's hearts.
idiomatic: If Your Majesty truly means to lay down worldly cares and dwell in clarity, the heir's charge should carry on the succession; but to discard the heir[1] and lightly move the throne—I fear that is not what the sages intended and will shock the realm.

literal: Moreover, all under Heaven is the ancestral temples' all under Heaven, and Your Majesty would on a whim alter the sacred vessel—above you would offend the seven temples and seven spirits, below you would lengthen the road of treason and disorder; this is where fortune and misfortune arise. I beg deep thought and caution.
idiomatic: Moreover, the realm belongs to the ancestral temples, not to a whim that shifts the sacred vessel—offending the seven temples above and feeding rebellion below. Fortune and ruin turn on such a step. I beg Your Majesty to weigh it deeply.

literal: Grand Commandant Yuan He also advanced and said: "Your Majesty now wishes to choose among the outer princes and abdicate to the imperial uncle—I fear that in spring and autumn offerings the zhao and mu lines will fall into disorder, and that ten thousand generations hence there will surely be the reproach of inverted sacrifice. I deeply wish you to ponder the Prince of Rencheng's words."
idiomatic: Grand Commandant Yuan He added, "To choose an outer prince and abdicate to the imperial uncle will disorder the zhao and mu lines at the seasonal sacrifices and invite, ages hence, the reproach of inverted rites. I beg Your Majesty heed the Prince of Rencheng."

literal: Yuan Pi of Dongyang and others advanced and said: "The crown prince's sagely virtue was long manifest, yet in truth he is still very young."
idiomatic: Yuan Pi of Dongyang and others said, "The crown prince's virtue is plain, yet he is still a child."

literal: Your Majesty is in the prime of life and has only begun to survey state affairs; all under Heaven looks up in admiration, the whole realm inclines its heart. To exalt solitary goodness and not take the ten thousand things to heart—what of the ancestral temples, what of the hundred millions!"
idiomatic: Your Majesty is in your prime and has only begun to govern; the realm looks up to you. To seek private ease and ignore the ten thousand things—what becomes of the temples, what of the people?"

literal: Xianzu said: "The heir's palace is orthodox; he receives the end from Wenzu, and the lords assist him—what cannot be done?"
idiomatic: Xianzu said, "The heir holds the orthodox line, receives the mandate from Wenzu, and will have the lords' aid—what could be impossible?"

literal: Thereupon he passed the throne to Gaozu.
idiomatic: Thereupon he abdicated to Gaozu.

literal: Later, when the Rouran raided the frontier, Yun was made Grand Commander of the Center Army and followed Xianzu to campaign; they met on the Great Marsh.
idiomatic: When the Rouran raided the frontier Yun was made Grand Commander of the Center Army, followed Xianzu to war, and met them on the Great Marsh.

literal: The affair is given in full in the Rouran biography.
idiomatic: The campaign is recorded in the Rouran biography.

literal: Later the Di of Chouchi rebelled; Yun was made Grand General Who Conquers the West and pacified them.
idiomatic: When the Chouchi Di rebelled he was made Grand General Who Conquers the West and pacified them.

literal: He was removed and made commander of all military affairs along the Huai on Xu and Yan provinces, Grand General Who Conquers the East, with an open office, and Inspector of Xuzhou.
idiomatic: He was then made commander of Huai-border armies in Xu and Yan, Grand General Who Conquers the East with an open office, and inspector of Xuzhou.

literal: When his grand consort Lady Gai died,[2] Yun memorialized asking to resign his post. Prince of Nan'an, Prince of Chengyang, Prince of Zhangwu, Prince of Leling, Prince of Anding
idiomatic: When his grand consort Lady Gai died,[2] Yun asked to resign. What follows: the Princes of Nan'an, Chengyang, Zhangwu, Leling, and Anding

literal: Zhen, Prince Hui of Nan'an
idiomatic: Zhen, Prince Hui of Nan'an

literal: Zhen, Prince of Nan'an, was enfeoffed in the second year of Huangxing, appointed Grand General Who Conquers the South and Director of the Inner Palace at the Center, and soon transferred to Director of the Inner Palace within the capital.
idiomatic: Zhen, Prince of Nan'an, was enfeoffed in Huangxing year 2, made Grand General Who Conquers the South and Director of the Inner Palace at the Center, and soon moved to the inner directorate.

literal: When Gaozu took the throne, he was made Grand General of Liangzhou Garrison.
idiomatic: At Gaozu's accession he was made commander of Liangzhou Garrison.

literal: Soon, for able pacification, he was added commander of all military affairs of the Western Rong, Grand General Who Conquers the West, Protector-General of the Western Regions, Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Inspector of Liangzhou.
idiomatic: Soon, for skill in pacification, he was added commander of Western Rong armies, Grand General Who Conquers the West, Protector-General of the Western Regions, Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies, and inspector of Liangzhou.

literal: He was summoned as Director of the Inner Palace within the capital, then sent out as Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, his former rank, with an open office, Grand General of Chang'an Garrison, and Inspector of Yongzhou.
idiomatic: He was recalled to the inner directorate, then sent out as Bearer of the Staff and Palace Attendant with his former rank, an open office, command of Chang'an Garrison, and the Yongzhou inspectorate.

literal: Zhen was by nature loyal and careful; he served his mother with a fame for filial piety and was rewarded with a thousand bolts of silk in praise.
idiomatic: Zhen was loyal and careful, famed for filial service to his mother; the court gave him a thousand bolts of silk in praise.

literal: Summoned to the martial review, Gaozu received him in the Hall of Imperial Trust and admonished him: "Sir, your filial conduct is manifest in the private hall and your fair name shines in the state—each time I admire your loyal goodness I wish to speak with you at length; therefore at the martial review I summoned you from afar to the court.
idiomatic: Called to the martial review, Gaozu received him in the Hall of Imperial Trust and warned him: "Your filial conduct shines at home and your fair name in the realm; I have long wished to hear you speak, and so at the review I summoned you from afar.

literal: I look up in longing for your kindness; the feeling in my heart is not yet spent.
idiomatic: I still yearn for your counsel; my heart is not satisfied.

literal: But Chang'an Garrison has had famine these years and the people are straitened; it must be pacified and cannot long keep you here. Sir, return now to your province and work diligently to comfort and pity—let there be no hungry people within your borders.
idiomatic: Yet Chang'an has known famine and the people are straitened; the post must be pacified and cannot keep you long. Return to your province, comfort the hidden poor, and let no one within your borders go hungry.

literal: As a great kin of the state you will in the end have no worry of poverty.
idiomatic: As a prince of the blood you need never fear want.

literal: What you should guard against are roughly three things: first, relying on kinship to be proud and arrogant, violating ritual and overstepping measure;
idiomatic: What you must guard against are three things: first, pride of kinship that breaks ritual and oversteps bounds;

literal: second, arrogance, greed, and luxury without pity for government;
idiomatic: second, arrogance, greed, and luxury without care for government;

literal: third, wine-drinking, roaming, and pleasure without choosing companions.
idiomatic: third, wine, wandering, and careless company.

literal: If these three are not cast off, misfortune will be born; if you can be careful in these, it is enough to preserve the body, keep harm far off, and bring glory to the state and honor to the house—the virtue of beginning and end will be complete.
idiomatic: If you do not cast these off, ruin will follow; if you heed them, you may keep your person safe, harm at bay, and bring honor to throne and house from first to last."

literal: " Yet Zhen could not follow and obey; afterward he gathered wealth at will.
idiomatic: Zhen could not obey; afterward he amassed wealth as he pleased.

literal: Empress Dowager Wenming and Gaozu both came to the Hall of Imperial Trust and received the kings and dukes; the empress dowager ordered: "The Prince of Ruyin, Tiansi, and the Prince of Nan'an, Zhen, do not follow the law; they profane goods and gather wealth. By the statutes they should be judged and sit in peril beyond measure.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Wenming and Gaozu received the princes in the Hall of Imperial Trust. The empress dowager said, "Prince Tiansi of Ruyin and Prince Zhen of Nan'an break the law, profane office, and hoard wealth. By statute they face death.

literal: Will you lords preserve kin and ruin the ordinance, or destroy kin to clarify the law?"
idiomatic: Will you preserve kin and ruin the law, or destroy kin to make the law plain?"

literal: The ministers all said the two princes bore the former emperor's body and should receive compassion and pardon.
idiomatic: The ministers all said both princes bore Gaozong's flesh and should be spared.

literal: The empress dowager did not answer.
idiomatic: The empress dowager did not reply.

literal: Gaozu then issued an edict: "The Prince of Nan'an, Zhen, by the honor of close kin, held command west of the Pass; he could not cleanse himself and serve the public, help proclaim the imperial measure, but instead indulged greed, heaped goods in his private hall, released wicked prisoners, blocked suits at law, bribed envoys, and sought empty praise—two or three such counts all violate the penal code.
idiomatic: Gaozu then decreed: "Prince Zhen of Nan'an, by grace of close kin, held the west of the Pass yet would not keep himself clean or aid the throne's measure; he indulged greed, stocked his private hall, freed wicked prisoners, blocked suits, bribed envoys, and sought empty praise—each count violates the penal code.

literal: Formerly Cao Cao of Wei cut his hair to align the host; Shuqiu Xiang killed his younger brother to clarify the law—restraining oneself and bearing kin away to lead all under Heaven.
idiomatic: Cao Cao of Wei once cut his hair to discipline the army; Shuqiu Xiang killed his brother to clarify the law—men who restrained themselves and bore kin away to lead the realm.

literal: Was it that they did not cherish them? They had business and acted thus.
idiomatic: Did they not love them? They had a duty and acted.

literal: Today's offenses weigh heavier than yesterday's; following antiquity and pushing punishment, in truth they are hard to pardon.
idiomatic: Today's crimes outweigh yesterday's; by ancient precedent punishment is hard to spare.

literal: The empress dowager's heavenly kindness is broad and deep; in pity for the state's kin, each time she searches her thoughts on Gaozong's close embrace nearby, her words choke and grief fills her breast;
idiomatic: The empress dowager's kindness is deep; pitying the imperial kin, each time she thinks of Gaozong's close embrace her words choke and grief fills her;

literal: and because the Prince of Nan'an's name for filial nurture is heard within and without;
idiomatic: and because Prince Zhen of Nan'an is famed within and without for filial care;

literal: she has specially granted one pardon, struck off his enfeoffment, and sent him home as a commoner, confined for life."
idiomatic: she has granted one pardon: his title is struck off, he returns home a commoner, and is confined for life."

literal: Later, when Gaozu campaigned south, Zhen followed to Luoyang; when the move of the capital was debated he was first to follow the great plan, and Gaozu was greatly pleased.
idiomatic: When Gaozu marched south Zhen followed to Luoyang; at the debate over moving the capital he was first to endorse the great plan, and Gaozu was greatly pleased.

literal: When Zhen's mother Grand Consort Liu died, Gaozu personally went to console him.
idiomatic: When his mother Grand Consort Liu died, Gaozu went in person to console him.

literal: At the burial he was given five hundred lengths of cloth and silk.
idiomatic: At the burial he was given five hundred lengths of cloth and silk.

literal: Again, because Zhen had settled the plan to move the capital, he was re-created Prince of Nan'an with a fief of a thousand households.
idiomatic: Because he had helped settle the capital move, he was re-created Prince of Nan'an with a thousand-household fief.

literal: He was sent out as Grand General Who Guards the North and Inspector of Xiangzhou.
idiomatic: He was sent out as Grand General Who Guards the North and inspector of Xiangzhou.

literal: Gaozu saw Zhen off at the Pavilion of the Imperial Grove.
idiomatic: Gaozu saw him off at the Pavilion of the Imperial Grove.

literal: An edict said: "My paternal uncle of Nan'an, now going to his frontier post, will soon be a thousand li apart; I forefeel regret and longing.
idiomatic: The edict read, "My paternal uncle of Nan'an goes to his frontier post; soon we shall be a thousand li apart, and I already feel regret.

literal: Yet today's gathering, though called a parting, is in truth a bent feast; all may compose poems to declare their hearts.
idiomatic: Yet today's gathering, though a farewell, is truly a feast bent to joy—all may compose poems to speak their hearts.

literal: Archery lets one view virtue; those who cannot compose poems may listen to the archery.
idiomatic: Archery reveals virtue; those who cannot write may watch the bow.

literal: Let warriors bend the bow and men of letters set brush to paper.
idiomatic: Let warriors bend the bow and scholars set brush to paper.

literal: " Gaozu escorted Zhen down the steps and parted with tears.
idiomatic: Gaozu walked him down the steps and parted in tears.

literal: In the fifth month of the twentieth year of Taihe he reached Ye; on the day he entered administration a violent wind and great rain struck, and several tens froze to death.
idiomatic: In Taihe year 20, fifth month, he reached Ye; on his first day in office a violent wind and great rain struck, and several tens died of cold.

literal: Zhen again prayed for rain to the host of spirits because of drought.
idiomatic: During drought he again prayed for rain to the host of spirits.

literal: In Ye city there was a Stone Tiger shrine that the people worshipped.
idiomatic: Ye had a Stone Tiger shrine that the people worshipped.

literal: Zhen addressed the Stone Tiger image and said: "If in three days there is no rain, I shall add the whip's punishment.
idiomatic: Zhen addressed the Stone Tiger image: "If there is no rain in three days, I shall add the whip's punishment.
